newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army resists rebels north east of Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army resists rebels north east of Kisangani.

text.p: Zaire reported heavy fighting between its army and rebels north east of the strategic third city of Kisangani on Friday, as the U.N. reported Rwandan Hutu refugees dying in jungles and rivers to the south.

Rebel sources in the east acknowledged that Zaire's motley army of Zairean regulars backed by Serb mercenaries and Rwandan Hutu hardliners was putting up stiff resistance around Kisangani, headquarters of army operations in the war zone.
"We have been making probing attacks towards Kisangani and they have met some resistance which we cannot ignore," one rebel source in the eastern border town of Goma said.

In Kinshasa, an opinion poll suggested that President Mobutu Sese Seko's popularity has plunged in the capital while a majority of those questioned admitted to a good opinion of rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

Critics said the poll was unrepresentative of Zaire as the capital was a traditional hotbed of opposition to Mobutu, who has spent most of his time in Europe since an operation for prostate cancer in Switzerland in August.
A senior supporter of Mobutu predicted that he would return to Zaire from his villa in the south of France on Monday.
A Defence Ministry spokesman reported heavy fighting between the army and rebels for two days around 80 km (50 miles) north east of Kisangani on the road from the town of Bafwasende.
"The Zairean armed forces destroyed a rebel command post and pushed the rebels back by another 10 km (six miles)," he said. "Among 35 rebels killed were a colonel and a major from the rebel forces."
In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said Hutu refugees were dying in Zaire's jungles and drowning while crossing rivers and expressed alarm at their plight as the rainy season begins.
Spokesman Kris Janowski said the rainy season would further complicate aid efforts in the remote rainforests of east Zaire, turning grass landing strips into mud.

Up to 100,000 hungry and exhausted refugees have arrived at the town of Ubundu on the Zaire River upstream from Kisangani after a long trek across the rainforest, fleeing advances by the mainly Tutsi rebels.
World Food Programme spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said a U.N. aid flight carrying food for refugees in Ubundu had to be cancelled on Friday because rains made landing impossible.

The rebels, who are also advancing in the key mining province of Shaba, took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu, who seized power in 1965. They accuse the authorities of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them.

Kabila, a native of Shaba, has seen his forces pile victory upon victory. He has rejected diplomatic pressure for a truce, most recently on Thursday when he met U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun in Uganda.

The Zaire-based consulting company, BERCI, which conducted the Kinshasa opinion poll and describes itself as independent, said Kabila fared well. "Almost 51 percent of those questioned have a good opinion of the rebel leader," BERCI said.
But few of those questioned earlier this month said they would vote for Kabila in an election.
BERCI said almost 73 per cent of those questioned had a "bad opinion" of Mobutu. This was the lowest since BERCI resumed political polling in 1995. No earlier figures were available.
